item.passage:
Thirty seconds of film, Ms. Varga had said, made entirely from still photographs. At twelve photographs to the second, that came to three hundred sixty pictures, and Ana had done the arithmetic on the bus before she and her partner, Felix, had even chosen a subject.

They chose a snail. On Saturday morning Felix rolled one from green clay at Ana's kitchen table, a thumb-sized body under a coiled shell striped in brown, and they set it at one end of a sheet of poster board with a pencil path curving across to the other. The method was simple. Move the snail the width of a grain of rice, take a picture with the phone propped on a stack of cookbooks, and move it again.

By eleven they had forty pictures. By noon they had ninety, and Ana wanted to start moving the snail two grains at a time.

"It'll look like it's hopping," Felix said. "Snails don't hop."

"Nobody watches a snail that closely," Ana said. But she kept to one grain.

At two o'clock they played back what they had. The snail slid forward smoothly, but the whole picture brightened and dimmed as it went, as though clouds were crossing the kitchen. They were. The table stood beside the window, and all morning the sky had been changing behind them, one photograph at a time.

Felix said that maybe it looked like weather, and that weather could be part of the story. Ana watched the flicker run through the clip twice. Then she got up, pulled the curtains shut, and switched on the lamp over the stove.

"From the beginning," she said. "All ninety."

They finished after dark. Ana's mother brought them sandwiches at six and found them both bent over the table, Felix reading out the frame count from a notebook and Ana nudging the snail along with the end of a toothpick. By the last picture the snail had crossed the whole poster board, a little more than two feet.

On Monday the films played one after another on the classroom screen. When the snail's turn came, Ana watched the class instead of the screen. She had checked the file three times that morning, and her hands were cold. The snail crossed the board in thirty seconds, steady as the hand of a clock, and the light around it held perfectly still.

Afterward Ms. Varga asked how long it had taken to make. Felix said about nine hours, counting the first try.

"A real snail," Ana added, "could cross that board in less than a quarter of an hour." A few people laughed. She had looked it up the night before, and she said it as though it were the best part of the whole project.

item.passage:
In March they raised it in a single day,
one yellow section bolted on another
until it stood above the empty lot,
taller than anything else on our street.

At seven every morning a figure in an orange vest
crosses the mud and starts up the ladder
inside the tower, small as a stitch
traveling up a seam, and does not stop
until the cab door closes overhead.

Then the long arm wakes and swings,
and lowers its hook to the ground,
and lifts a bundle of steel beams as gently
as my grandmother lifts the lid from a pot
to see whether the rice is done.

I watch from the window over my homework.
What does a person eat up there at noon?
Is there a radio? A photograph taped
beside the levers? On windy days
does the whole cab sway like a branch?

By June the building reaches the fourth floor,
by August the ninth, each floor a gray shelf
the hook has filled. The crane climbs with it,
adding a piece to itself when no one is watching,
the way, my mother says, I grow.

In October they take it down in sections,
the arm, the cab, the long ladder of the tower,
onto trucks that leave before I am up.
Now there are windows where the sky was,
forty of them, lit in the evening,

and behind each one someone is cooking
or reading or setting down a bag,
already at home in rooms
that hung from a hook in May.

Some nights one of them stands at the glass
and looks across the street at our building,
at my window, at me, the way I looked
all year at the cab, and I wonder
which of my questions they are asking.

The summer I was eleven, my grandfather kept thirty-two homing pigeons in a loft he had built on the flat roof of his garage. It was a wooden room the size of a closet, painted white, with a wire porch on the front and a narrow shelf below the porch that he called the landing board. Every bird in the loft had hatched there, and every bird, he told me on my first morning, would come back to that board from almost anywhere he let it go.

My job was water, feed, and the scraper, and the scraper took most of the morning. My grandfather worked beside me, talking to the birds the whole time in the low voice he used on the telephone with my mother, and he knew each one by its face. I could tell the white birds from the gray ones. He could tell the gray ones from each other, and he would point out a narrow eye ring or a darker bar across a wing until I could too, almost.

In July we began the training tosses. Early one Saturday he packed twelve birds into a wicker basket, and we drove twenty miles east to the empty parking lot of the county fairground. He set the basket on the asphalt, checked his watch, and lifted the lid. The birds went up in a clatter and circled twice, wider each time, and then all twelve turned west together as if someone had called them.

We drove home at the speed limit. Most of the birds were on the landing board before we pulled into the driveway.

One was missing, a gray hen with a white patch on her neck. I had named her Comma, for the shape of the patch, and had been calling her that out loud all week. My grandfather climbed the ladder to the roof with two folding chairs and a thermos, and we sat up there through the afternoon, facing east. He hardly talked. Every so often he lifted a hand to shade his eyes, then lowered it again.

At dinner I asked why we didn't drive back to the fairground and look for her. He said that you find a lost pigeon by waiting for it, and that looking only tires you out. Then he carried his plate up the ladder and finished eating on the roof.

She came in a little after seven, low over the neighbors' roofs, and landed on the board so hard that she skidded. My grandfather picked her up in both hands, turned her over, spread each wing in turn, and looked at her feet. Then he set her inside with the others and wrote something in the small notebook he kept in his shirt pocket.

Later he left the notebook open on the kitchen table, and I read the line. It gave the date, the time, 7:12, and one word: Comma.

The loft was sold years ago to a man in the next county who races pigeons. Still, on summer evenings, I sometimes catch myself facing east with a hand raised to shade my eyes, and then lowering it again.

The summer I was eleven, my grandfather kept thirty-two homing pigeons in a loft he had built on the flat roof of his garage. It was a wooden room the size of a closet, painted white, with a wire porch on the front and a narrow shelf below the porch that he called the landing board. Every bird in the loft had hatched there, and every bird, he told me on my first morning, would come back to that board from almost anywhere he let it go.

My job was water, feed, and the scraper, and the scraper took most of the morning. My grandfather worked beside me, talking to the birds the whole time in the low voice he used on the telephone with my mother, and he knew each one by its face. I could tell the white birds from the gray ones. He could tell the gray ones from each other, and he would point out a narrow eye ring or a darker bar across a wing until I could too, almost.

In July we began the training tosses. Early one Saturday he packed twelve birds into a wicker basket, and we drove twenty miles east to the empty parking lot of the county fairground. He set the basket on the asphalt, checked his watch, and lifted the lid. The birds went up in a clatter and circled twice, wider each time, and then all twelve turned west together as if someone had called them.

We drove home at the speed limit. Most of the birds were on the landing board before we pulled into the driveway.

One was missing, a gray hen with a white patch on her neck. I had named her Comma, for the shape of the patch, and had been calling her that out loud all week. My grandfather climbed the ladder to the roof with two folding chairs and a thermos, and we sat up there through the afternoon, facing east. He hardly talked. Every so often he lifted a hand to shade his eyes, then lowered it again.

At dinner I asked why we didn't drive back to the fairground and look for her. He said that you find a lost pigeon by waiting for it, and that looking only tires you out. Then he carried his plate up the ladder and finished eating on the roof.

She came in a little after seven, low over the neighbors' roofs, and landed on the board so hard that she skidded. At the elementary school near my house, recess lasts fifteen minutes. I know this because I can hear it from my kitchen: the bell, a rising roar of voices, and then, what seems like a moment later, the second bell and the slow quiet as the playground empties. Fifteen minutes sounds like a reasonable break. In practice it is much less.

Watch a recess closely and you will see why. The first few minutes go to coats, the line at the door, and the walk across the parking lot. The last few go to the whistle, the second line, and the walk back. What is left in the middle is perhaps eight minutes, and eight minutes is long enough for exactly one kind of play: running. Children sprint to the far fence and back, chase each other in loops, and are called inside still out of breath.

Running is good for them, and I would never argue otherwise. But it is the other kind of play that a short recess quietly removes. Give the same children forty minutes and something different happens. Around the twelfth minute, a group drifts toward the blacktop and starts a game of four square, and before the first ball is served they have spent five minutes arguing about the rules. Does a ball on the line count? Can you catch it, or only hit it? Who decides when two people disagree?

Adults tend to see that argument as time wasted. I think it is the most useful part of the whole day. In those five minutes, children are doing what a classroom has trouble teaching: making a rule, testing it against a hard case, changing it when it proves unfair, and living with it once it is agreed. They are, in a small way, writing a constitution for a square of painted asphalt. Eight minutes leaves room for the ball. It leaves no room for the argument.

The usual reason for shortening recess is that the time is needed for lessons, and the pressure behind that reason is real. Schools are asked to cover more each year, and minutes have to come from somewhere. But teachers who have tried longer breaks often report that the minutes come back. Children who have had a real break tend to settle more quickly and pay closer attention, so a lesson that begins after forty minutes outside may cover as much as one that begins after fifteen, with less effort spent getting everyone to sit down.

I am asking for something modest: enough time, once a day, for a game to need rules. Fifteen minutes is enough for children to burn off energy. Thirty or forty is enough for them to practice governing themselves, and that is a lesson worth the time it takes.

In 1909 the town of Esker Falls built a bandstand on its green. It was an eight-sided platform with a peaked roof and a railing of turned spindles, paid for by a subscription that ran out before anyone had bought the paint. For two years it stood the color of the bare pine it was made from, slowly going gray, while the town band played on it every other Saturday to audiences that rarely filled the first row of benches.

In the spring of 1911 the bandleader, a tinsmith named Otto Brauner, asked the town council for forty dollars to paint it. The council agreed at once. It was the color that started the trouble.

The Ladies' Improvement Society wanted white with green trim, to match the church across the green, and said that anything else would make the square look like a fairground. The band wanted red, the red of its uniform coats, and Brauner argued that a bandstand ought to be seen from the far end of Main Street. A third party, smaller but louder, wanted it left gray, on the grounds that the town had gotten used to it.

For six weeks the question filled the letters column of the Esker Falls Courier. One writer said that white was the only color a serious town painted anything. Another replied that a serious town would have finished its bandstand two years earlier. At the council's May meeting, which usually drew a handful of people, the room was full and the doors were propped open so that those standing in the hall could hear.

Mayor Ezra Pruett, mostly to get the question out of his council room, proposed to settle it at the Fourth of July concert. Every adult on the green would be handed a bean and could drop it into one of three jars set on the bandstand steps. Pruett himself predicted that the result would end nothing, and that the losing side would simply carry the matter back to the council in the fall.

On the Fourth the green held more people than anyone could remember seeing there. The band played for two hours. When the beans were counted, red had 212, white had 207, and gray had 31. Faced with a margin of five, the council ordered the platform and roof painted white and the railing red.

The losing side did not return in the fall. Concerts that summer and for some years afterward drew crowds that filled the benches and spilled onto the grass, many of them people who had first come to the green to cast a bean.

The bandstand has been repainted roughly once a decade since, always white with a red railing. The town has never voted on its color again. It has simply kept the colors the argument left behind.

On a summer evening over a lawn or the edge of a meadow, the small yellow-green flashes of fireflies can look like random sparks. They are closer to a conversation. Fireflies are beetles, and in many species the adults use their light chiefly for one purpose: to find a mate of the right kind in the dark.

The light itself comes from a chemical reaction in a special organ near the tip of the abdomen. There, a compound called luciferin combines with oxygen with the help of an enzyme called luciferase, and the reaction releases its energy mostly as light rather than as heat. A glowing firefly gives off very little warmth, which is why its glow is sometimes called cold light. Exactly how the insect switches the light on and off so quickly is still being studied, but it appears to depend on controlling how much oxygen reaches the light-producing cells.

What the flashes say depends on their pattern. In one common North American species, a male flies low over the grass at dusk and flashes about every five or six seconds, each flash a short upward swoop. A female perched on a grass blade below answers with a single flash of her own after a pause of roughly two seconds. The male turns toward her, flashes again, and waits for the reply. The exchange can repeat several times as he closes in.

Each species has its own code: the length of a flash, the number of pulses, the time between them, the shape a male traces in the air, and above all the delay before the female answers. Several species may fly over the same field on the same night, and the differences in timing let each insect pick out its own kind among dozens of blinking strangers. Flashing also tends to slow down on cool nights, for males and females alike, so the two stay roughly in step.

A code that can be read can also be copied. Females of one group of fireflies, known as Photuris, can imitate the answering flash of females from other species. When a male of another species flies down expecting a mate, the Photuris female catches and eats him. Researchers have found that she gains more than a meal: the males she eats carry defensive chemicals that make fireflies taste bad to spiders and other predators, and she takes those chemicals into her own body.

Scientists who study fireflies sometimes walk fields at night with a small penlight, flashing back at males in the pattern of a female. A good imitation can bring a male down to the light within seconds. That so simple a tool works so well is a reminder of how precise the original system is: a pause of a second or two, timed by a beetle in the dark, carries nearly everything the conversation needs.
